listening.title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak: When and where to catch a glimpse
listening.topic: The Perseid meteor shower reaches its annual peak, coinciding with a partial solar eclipse for an exceptional night of stargazing.
listening.topic_zh: 英仙座流星雨迎來年度高峰，同時與日偏食重合，形成一個絕佳的觀星夜。
listening.transcript_excerpt: Every year, skywatchers around the world eagerly await the return of the Perseid meteor shower — widely regarded as one of the most spectacular annual astronomical events. This year, the Perseids are particularly special. Not only is the meteor shower peaking on Wednesday night, but it also coincides with a deep partial solar eclipse visible from the United Kingdom, creating what astronomer Dr Becky Smethurst called 'the perfect cosmic coincidence of events'. The Perseids are caused by debris left behind by the Swift-Tuttle comet, a large comet whose solid core measures approximately 16 miles across. As the Earth passes through this trail of frozen rock and gas, the fragments enter our atmosphere and burn up, producing those breathtaking streaks of light we call meteors. What makes this year's display even more impressive is the timing of a new moon, meaning there will be virtually no moonlight to wash out the fainter meteors in the night sky. Dr Smethurst described the Perseids as 'one of the best nights for astronomy all year', and with Swift-Tuttle taking 133 years to complete a single orbit around the Sun, some of the debris burning up tonight may have been drifting through space for over a century. It really is, as she put it, the Universe's own cosmic clock.

vocabulary.definition: A celestial event in which numerous meteors are observed radiating from one point in the night sky, caused by Earth passing through a stream of debris from a comet or asteroid.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 流星雨，指地球穿過彗星或小行星留下的碎片帶時，大量流星從天空某一輻射點向外射出的天文現象。
vocabulary.example: Thousands of people travelled to rural areas to witness the annual meteor shower away from city light pollution.

vocabulary.definition: Scattered fragments or remnants, particularly pieces of rock or ice left behind by a comet or asteroid as it travels through space.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 碎片，尤指彗星或小行星在太空中移動時留下的岩石或冰塊殘骸。
vocabulary.example: As the comet passed close to the Sun, it shed a trail of debris that would later create a stunning meteor display.

vocabulary.definition: To occur at the same time or to correspond exactly with another event; to happen simultaneously.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 同時發生，指兩個或多個事件在時間或空間上重合。
vocabulary.example: The festival was planned to coincide with the summer solstice to maximise visitor numbers.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to astronomy or celestial bodies; also used figuratively to describe something enormously large or significant.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 天文學的，與天文學或天體有關的；也可引申為極大的或極重要的。
vocabulary.example: The astronomical cost of launching satellites into orbit has historically limited space exploration to wealthy nations.

vocabulary.definition: To make something difficult to see, hear, or understand by covering or blocking it; to conceal or hide from view.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 遮蔽，使某物難以看見或理解；掩蓋或阻擋視線。
vocabulary.example: Heavy cloud cover threatened to obscure the eclipse from viewers across the northern regions.

questions.q: What makes this year's Perseid meteor shower particularly exceptional according to the passage?
options: A: It is expected to produce more meteors than in any previous year
B: It coincides with a partial solar eclipse and a new moon on the same night
C: The Swift-Tuttle comet will be visible to the naked eye for the first time
D: It can only be seen from the United Kingdom this year
questions.explanation: The passage states that a deep partial solar eclipse is also visible in the UK on the same evening, and that the new moon means no bright moonlight will obscure the meteors, making it an exceptional combination of events.

questions.q: How long does the Swift-Tuttle comet take to complete one orbit around the Sun?
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that Swift-Tuttle takes 133 years to complete a single orbit around the Sun, which is why some debris burning up in our atmosphere may have been left behind more than a century ago.

questions.q: What does Dr Becky Smethurst mean when she calls the Perseids 'the Universe's own cosmic clock'?
options: A: The shower helps scientists measure the exact speed of comets
B: The recurring annual event marks the passage of time in a predictable, cyclical way
C: The meteors can be used to calculate the age of the solar system
D: The shower only occurs at midnight, making it useful for timekeeping
questions.explanation: Dr Smethurst uses the metaphor of a cosmic clock to suggest that the Perseids return reliably every year, creating a natural, cyclical rhythm that marks the passage of time, much like a clock.

reading.title: The Science and Significance of Annual Meteor Showers
reading.passage:
Each year, the night sky is illuminated by a series of predictable meteor showers, the most celebrated of which is the Perseid meteor shower, which peaks reliably in mid-August. These events are not random occurrences but are the result of a well-understood astronomical mechanism: as the Earth completes its annual orbit around the Sun, it periodically intersects the debris trails left behind by comets and, less commonly, asteroids. When these fragments of rock and ice — often no larger than a grain of sand — enter the Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 70 kilometres per second, they superheat and vaporise, producing the luminous streaks of light commonly referred to as meteors or, colloquially, shooting stars.

The Perseids derive their name from the constellation Perseus, from which the meteors appear to radiate when observed from Earth. They are produced by debris shed by the comet Swift-Tuttle, a notably large comet with a solid nucleus measuring approximately 26 kilometres in diameter. Swift-Tuttle completes one full orbit around the Sun every 133 years, meaning that the fragments currently burning up in Earth's atmosphere may have been released into space well over a century ago. This temporal dimension lends the event a profound sense of cosmic scale that few other natural phenomena can match.

This year's Perseid display is considered especially favourable for several reasons. First, the peak coincides with a new moon phase, which eliminates the interfering brightness of moonlight and significantly enhances the visibility of fainter meteors. Second, and quite remarkably, a deep partial solar eclipse is also occurring over the United Kingdom on the same evening, providing skywatchers with two distinct and unrelated celestial spectacles within a matter of hours. Astronomers have emphasised that while the two events are entirely coincidental, their simultaneous occurrence represents an extraordinary opportunity for both amateur and professional observation. Under optimal viewing conditions — clear skies, minimal light pollution, and a location away from urban centres — observers may witness up to 100 meteors per hour at peak activity.

questions.statement: The Perseid meteor shower is caused by debris from the Swift-Tuttle comet, which orbits the Sun every 133 years.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that the Perseids are produced by debris shed by comet Swift-Tuttle, which completes one full orbit around the Sun every 133 years.

questions.statement: The partial solar eclipse and the Perseid meteor shower are astronomically related phenomena that occur together by design.
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that 'the two events are entirely coincidental' and describes them as 'unrelated celestial spectacles', directly contradicting the idea that they are related or occur by design.

questions.statement: Amateur astronomers are advised to use telescopes to achieve the best viewing experience during the Perseid peak.
questions.explanation: While the passage mentions optimal viewing conditions such as clear skies and minimal light pollution, it does not mention whether telescopes are recommended or advised for viewing the meteor shower.

questions.q: According to the passage, what primarily causes a meteor to produce a streak of light in the sky?
options: A: The reflection of sunlight off the surface of cometary debris
B: A chemical reaction between comet fragments and atmospheric oxygen
C: The superheating and vaporisation of debris as it enters the atmosphere at high speed
D: The gravitational compression of rock fragments as they approach Earth's surface
questions.explanation: The passage states that fragments 'enter the Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 70 kilometres per second, they superheat and vaporise, producing the luminous streaks of light', making option C the correct answer.

speaking.topic: Describe a natural event or phenomenon that you found particularly impressive or memorable.
speaking.topic_zh: 描述一個你覺得特別令人印象深刻或難忘的自然現象或事件。

part2.cue_card:
Describe a natural event or phenomenon that you found particularly impressive or memorable.

You should say:
• What the natural event or phenomenon was
• When and where you experienced or learned about it
• What made it so impressive or memorable to you

And explain how it affected your feelings or your view of the natural world.
band_tips: Use sophisticated astronomical and scientific vocabulary naturally, such as 'celestial', 'orbit', 'debris trail', and 'phenomenon', to demonstrate a wide lexical range and boost your Lexical Resource score.

Employ a range of narrative tenses accurately — past simple for the event itself, past continuous for background atmosphere, and past perfect to describe prior knowledge — to showcase your Grammatical Range and Accuracy.

Develop your response with layered reflection: describe the sensory experience first, then your emotional reaction, and finally the broader philosophical or scientific significance it held for you, which demonstrates coherent discourse organisation and personal depth.

part3.q: Why do you think people are so fascinated by astronomical events such as meteor showers or eclipses?
part3.q_zh: 你認為為什麼人們對流星雨或日食等天文現象如此著迷？
key_points: Astronomical events trigger a sense of awe and remind us of our relative smallness within a vast universe, satisfying a deep human need for wonder and perspective.
Unlike many natural spectacles, meteor showers and eclipses are predictable yet still feel miraculous, combining scientific understanding with genuine emotional impact.
In an increasingly screen-dominated world, stargazing offers a rare form of collective, technology-free experience that encourages communities to gather and look upward together.

part3.q: Do you think governments should invest more funding in space exploration and astronomical research? Why or why not?
part3.q_zh: 你認為政府應該在太空探索和天文研究上投入更多資金嗎？為什麼？
key_points: Proponents argue that space research has historically yielded transformative spin-off technologies — from satellite navigation to medical imaging — that justify the enormous initial investment.
Critics contend that urgent terrestrial issues such as climate change, poverty, and public health should take priority over what they perceive as the abstract benefits of deep-space exploration.

A balanced perspective recognises that space science and Earth-based challenges are not mutually exclusive, as climate monitoring satellites and asteroid tracking programmes directly serve human welfare.

part3.q: How has technology changed the way ordinary people engage with and learn about natural sciences like astronomy?
part3.q_zh: 科技如何改變了普通人參與和學習天文學等自然科學的方式？
key_points: Citizen science platforms and smartphone applications now allow amateur enthusiasts to contribute meaningfully to professional research, democratising participation in what was once a highly specialist field.

Live-streaming technology and social media have transformed astronomical events into shared global experiences, enabling people without access to clear skies or telescopes to observe phenomena virtually in real time.

However, increased screen time and digital distraction may paradoxically reduce the number of people who step outside to experience the night sky directly, creating a tension between digital access and authentic engagement.

part3.q: Some people argue that science education in schools focuses too much on theory and not enough on inspiring wonder about the natural world. Do you agree?
part3.q_zh: 有些人認為學校的科學教育過於注重理論，而沒有足夠地激發學生對自然世界的好奇心。你同意嗎？
key_points: A purely theoretical, examination-driven curriculum can alienate students who might otherwise develop a passionate interest in science if exposed to hands-on experiments, field trips, or events like meteor shower observations.

Inspiring wonder and building rigorous theoretical foundations are not mutually exclusive goals; the most effective science educators consistently demonstrate that curiosity and analytical discipline reinforce one another.

Cultural and resource disparities mean that access to experiential science education is often unevenly distributed, with students in well-funded urban schools receiving far richer practical opportunities than those in under-resourced communities.

writing.task2_question: Some people believe that governments should prioritise funding for space exploration and astronomical research, while others argue that this money would be better spent addressing problems on Earth such as poverty and climate change. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
writing.task2_question_zh: 一些人認為政府應優先為太空探索和天文研究提供資金，而另一些人則認為這些資金最好用於解決地球上的問題，如貧困和氣候變遷。討論兩種觀點並給出你自己的意見。

useful_phrases.phrase: Proponents of this view contend that...
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to introduce and attribute arguments to supporters of one side in a discussion essay, maintaining academic objectivity.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於在討論型文章中介紹並歸納某一方支持者的論點，保持學術客觀性。
useful_phrases.example: Proponents of this view contend that investment in astronomical research generates technological innovations that benefit society far beyond the laboratory.

useful_phrases.phrase: While the merits of this argument are undeniable, it overlooks the fact that...
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to acknowledge the validity of the opposing argument before introducing a counter-argument or refutation, demonstrating critical thinking.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於在提出反駁或反論之前承認對方論點的合理性，展現批判性思維。
useful_phrases.example: While the merits of this argument are undeniable, it overlooks the fact that many space research programmes directly contribute to Earth-based environmental monitoring.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to introduce a broadly accepted fact or consensus view at the start of a body paragraph to establish common ground before developing a specific argument.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於在段落開頭引入廣泛認可的事實或共識，在展開具體論點前建立共同基礎。
useful_phrases.example: It is widely acknowledged that the gap between the world's wealthiest and most impoverished nations continues to widen despite decades of international aid initiatives.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to shift the discussion toward future consequences or extended timeframes, which is particularly effective when arguing for investments that have delayed but significant returns.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於將討論轉向未來後果或更長的時間框架，尤其適合論證那些回報延遲但重要的投資。
useful_phrases.example: From a long-term perspective, the technologies derived from space exploration may ultimately prove indispensable in humanity's efforts to combat climate change.

useful_phrases.phrase: On balance, I would argue that...
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use in the conclusion or to signal your personal stance in a discussion essay, indicating that you have weighed both sides and reached a considered, measured judgment.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於討論型文章的結論或表明個人立場時，表示你已權衡雙方並得出深思熟慮的判斷。
useful_phrases.example: On balance, I would argue that a proportional investment in both space research and terrestrial welfare programmes represents the most pragmatic and ethical approach.

outline.intro: Begin by contextualising the debate with a broad statement about the competing demands on government budgets in the modern era. Paraphrase the question to demonstrate understanding, briefly outline both perspectives, and end with a clear thesis statement indicating that you will argue for a balanced, proportional approach to funding both domains.
outline.body1: Present the case for prioritising Earth-based spending. Argue that acute humanitarian crises — including extreme poverty, inadequate healthcare infrastructure, and accelerating climate change — demand immediate resource allocation. Acknowledge the moral weight of addressing visible, present-day human suffering and use specific examples such as climate adaptation funding or pandemic preparedness to illustrate the urgency. Concede that the benefits of space exploration, while real, are often abstract and long-term compared to these pressing needs.
outline.body2: Present the case for continued and increased investment in space and astronomical research. Argue that such investment is not purely academic: satellite technology underpins modern weather forecasting, GPS navigation, and climate monitoring, all of which directly serve Earth's population. Highlight how historical space programmes generated transformative spin-off technologies, and assert that asteroid detection and planetary science may one day prove critical to human survival. Argue that framing the debate as either-or is a false dichotomy, as both investment streams can coexist through strategic budgetary planning.
outline.conclusion: Restate your balanced position clearly and concisely without introducing new arguments. Emphasise that the most responsible governmental approach is to allocate funding proportionally rather than exclusively, ensuring that immediate human needs are met while the long-term scientific and technological investments that space research provides are not abandoned. End with a forward-looking statement about humanity's dual responsibility to its present and its future.
